# AssetToken: Tokenisation Using Blockchain

An academic dApp for NTU SC4053. Authorised issuers tokenise fictional real-world and digital assets as ERC-20 tokens and sell them at a fixed price to whitelisted investors. All ownership records and compliance rules live on Ethereum. The repository is also graded on how the AI-written code was audited, so every change carries an evidence trail (see [Audit trail](#audit-trail)).

**Status (4 November 2026):** contracts, frontend and local tests are complete. Two things remain: a genuine MetaMask browser check ([AUD-002](docs/issues/AUD-002-frontend-dashboards-and-wallet-integration-are-uni.md)) and the public Sepolia deployment ([AUD-003](docs/issues/AUD-003-deployment-and-verification-tooling-are-incomplete.md)).

## What it does

| Contract | Role |
|---|---|
| `AssetFactory` | The platform admin authorises or revokes issuers. An authorised issuer creates an asset, which deploys an `AssetToken` and an `AssetSale` and records them in the registry (`getAsset`, `getAssetCount`). |
| `AssetToken` | A fixed-supply ERC-20 with 0 decimals. Every transfer requires a whitelisted sender and recipient. Revoking an investor keeps their balance but blocks sending, receiving and buying. The issuer can **pause** all token movement and **force-transfer** tokens out of a revoked address, for example to recover a lost key (decision D5). |
| `AssetSale` | Holds sale inventory and sells it at a fixed price, with exact ETH payment. The issuer withdraws proceeds, closes the sale and recovers unsold tokens. ETH forced in from outside can be swept. |

The frontend (React 18, Vite, ethers 6) has a marketplace, an investor portfolio with transfers, issuer and admin dashboards, and on-chain transaction history. The specification is [`docs/spec/spec-v1.md`](docs/spec/spec-v1.md). Where the later phase requirements in [`docs/spec/`](docs/spec/) differ from it, those requirements and their recorded decisions (D1–D10) govern.

## Setup

Validated with Node 22.18.0 (macOS) and Node 24.15.0 with npm 11 (Windows). From the repository root:

```bash
npm ci
npm ci --prefix frontend
npm run compile
```

## Run locally

Use three terminals, all started in the repository root:

```bash
# Terminal 1: leave the local blockchain running
npm run node
```

```bash
# Terminal 2: deploy to that persistent chain and sync ABIs/configuration
npm run deploy:local

# Optional: seed CPT/DLT for exploration, only on an empty local registry
npm run demo:local
```

```bash
# Terminal 3: start the frontend
npm run dev --prefix frontend
```

Open **http://127.0.0.1:5173**. You can browse without a wallet. To sign transactions, connect MetaMask and switch to **Local Ethereum**: chain **31337**, RPC **http://127.0.0.1:8545**, symbol **ETH**. The app offers to add this network when you ask to switch.

Use Hardhat local accounts 0–4 for the admin, the issuer, investor 1, investor 2 and an unapproved investor. Only import these development accounts into a separate development wallet or profile. Hardhat prints their publicly known keys in your terminal; never use them for real funds or commit them. The application never asks for, stores or reads wallet private keys or seed phrases.

Every deployment writes `frontend/src/config/addresses.json` and syncs the three compiled ABIs. After restarting or resetting the chain, deploy again and restart Vite. The app checks the deployment's block hash and runtime bytecode hash, not just its address. `npm run deploy:ephemeral` deploys to a throwaway in-process chain instead.

The UI has no pause or forced-transfer controls (spec-v1 §7 does not require them). The issuer calls them directly on the token contract. Forced transfers do appear in the transaction history.

## Tests

```bash
npm test                              # 132 contract tests
npm test --prefix frontend            # 113 frontend behaviour tests
npm run build --prefix frontend       # TypeScript + production Vite build
npx tsc --noEmit                      # root scripts and contract tests
npm run test:integration              # needs `npm run node` running; deploys its own fixture
bash scripts/evidence.sh <label>      # build, test, gas, coverage (slither if installed) into docs/evidence/runs/
```

The integration suite runs the production frontend services against real local contracts. It signs through an EIP-1193 adapter over Hardhat's unlocked accounts, so it does not test MetaMask. It covers the full lifecycle, including a forced transfer and a pause. The counts above are from 4 November 2026. Contract line coverage is 98.79%.

## Sepolia deployment

```bash
npm run deploy:sepolia
```

This builds with the optimised `production` profile (AUD-012). Every profile has the optimizer on (AUD-014): unoptimised, `AssetFactory` is right at the 24 576-byte EIP-170 limit, because it embeds the other two contracts. `hardhat.config.ts` reads `TESTNET_RPC_URL` and `PRIVATE_KEY` with `configVariable`, from environment variables or Hardhat's encrypted keystore (`npx hardhat keystore set PRIVATE_KEY`). Nothing loads a `.env` file automatically; [`.env.example`](.env.example) lists the names. Use a testnet burner wallet only.

## Audit trail

AI tools (Claude Code, Codex, claude.ai) wrote most of the code. [`CLAUDE.md`](CLAUDE.md) sets the rules every AI session follows, including rules learned from each audit finding.

| Where | What |
|---|---|
| [`docs/issues/INDEX.md`](docs/issues/INDEX.md) | AUD-001 to AUD-014. Each defect has a failing test commit, a fix commit, before/after evidence and an analysis of why the AI made the mistake |
| [`docs/ai-logs/INDEX.md`](docs/ai-logs/INDEX.md) | Every AI session: tool, model, context given and outcome. Transcripts are in `docs/ai-logs/raw/` (emails and Hardhat dev keys redacted, decisions D9 and D10) |
| Tags `spec-v0`, `ai-baseline-phase2`, `-phase3`, `-phase4`, `-d5` | The pre-AI spec, and each first complete AI generation, never edited afterwards |
| [`docs/evidence/`](docs/evidence/) | Evidence runs and per-issue logs |
| [`docs/report/REPORT-MAP.md`](docs/report/REPORT-MAP.md) | Which evidence backs each section of the AI Audit Report |

Commit prefixes show who wrote what: `ai:`, `human:`, `test(AUD-NNN):`, `fix(AUD-NNN):`, `docs:`, `evidence:`, `chore:`. Implementation notes: [Phase 2](docs/phase2-implementation.md), [Phase 3](docs/phase3-implementation.md), [Phase 4](docs/phase4-implementation.md), [D5](docs/d5-implementation.md).

Academic demonstration only. Assets and token prices are simulated. Tokens do not represent legally enforceable ownership or investment claims.

# AssetToken: Tokenisation Using Blockchain

An academic dApp for NTU SC4053. Authorised issuers tokenise fictional real-world and digital assets as ERC-20 tokens and sell them at a fixed price to whitelisted investors. All ownership records and compliance rules live on Ethereum. The repository is also graded on how the AI-written code was audited, so every change carries an evidence trail (see [Audit trail](#audit-trail)).

**Status (4 November 2026):** contracts, frontend and local tests are complete. Two things remain: a genuine MetaMask browser check ([AUD-002](docs/issues/AUD-002-frontend-dashboards-and-wallet-integration-are-uni.md)) and the public Sepolia deployment ([AUD-003](docs/issues/AUD-003-deployment-and-verification-tooling-are-incomplete.md)).

## What it does

| Contract | Role |
|---|---|
| `AssetFactory` | The platform admin authorises or revokes issuers. An authorised issuer creates an asset, which deploys an `AssetToken` and an `AssetSale` and records them in the registry (`getAsset`, `getAssetCount`). |
| `AssetToken` | A fixed-supply ERC-20 with 0 decimals. Every transfer requires a whitelisted sender and recipient. Revoking an investor keeps their balance but blocks sending, receiving and buying. The issuer can **pause** all token movement and **force-transfer** tokens out of a revoked address, for example to recover a lost key (decision D5). |
| `AssetSale` | Holds sale inventory and sells it at a fixed price, with exact ETH payment. The issuer withdraws proceeds, closes the sale and recovers unsold tokens. ETH forced in from outside can be swept. |

The frontend (React 18, Vite, ethers 6) has a marketplace, an investor portfolio with transfers, issuer and admin dashboards, and on-chain transaction history. The specification is [`docs/spec/spec-v1.md`](docs/spec/spec-v1.md). Where the later phase requirements in [`docs/spec/`](docs/spec/) differ from it, those requirements and their recorded decisions (D1–D10) govern.

## Setup

Validated with Node 22.18.0 (macOS) and Node 24.15.0 with npm 11 (Windows). From the repository root:

```bash
npm ci
npm ci --prefix frontend
npm run compile
```

## Run locally

Use three terminals, all started in the repository root:

```bash
# Terminal 1: leave the local blockchain running
npm run node
```

```bash
# Terminal 2: deploy to that persistent chain and sync ABIs/configuration
npm run deploy:local

# Optional: seed CPT/DLT for exploration, only on an empty local registry
npm run demo:local
```

```bash
# Terminal 3: start the frontend
npm run dev --prefix frontend
```

Open **http://127.0.0.1:5173**. You can browse without a wallet. To sign transactions, connect MetaMask and switch to **Local Ethereum**: chain **31337**, RPC **http://127.0.0.1:8545**, symbol **ETH**. The app offers to add this network when you ask to switch.

Use Hardhat local accounts 0–4 for the admin, the issuer, investor 1, investor 2 and an unapproved investor. Only import these development accounts into a separate development wallet or profile. Hardhat prints their publicly known keys in your terminal; never use them for real funds or commit them. The application never asks for, stores or reads wallet private keys or seed phrases.

Every deployment writes `frontend/src/config/addresses.json` and syncs the three compiled ABIs. After restarting or resetting the chain, deploy again and restart Vite. The app checks the deployment's block hash and runtime bytecode hash, not just its address. `npm run deploy:ephemeral` deploys to a throwaway in-process chain instead.

The UI has no pause or forced-transfer controls (spec-v1 §7 does not require them). The issuer calls them directly on the token contract. Forced transfers do appear in the transaction history.

## Tests

```bash
npm test                              # 132 contract tests
npm test --prefix frontend            # 113 frontend behaviour tests
npm run build --prefix frontend       # TypeScript + production Vite build
npx tsc --noEmit                      # root scripts and contract tests
npm run test:integration              # needs `npm run node` running; deploys its own fixture
bash scripts/evidence.sh <label>      # build, test, gas, coverage (slither if installed) into docs/evidence/runs/
```

The integration suite runs the production frontend services against real local contracts. It signs through an EIP-1193 adapter over Hardhat's unlocked accounts, so it does not test MetaMask. It covers the full lifecycle, including a forced transfer and a pause. The counts above are from 4 November 2026. Contract line coverage is 98.79%.

## Sepolia deployment

```bash
npm run deploy:sepolia
```

This builds with the optimised `production` profile (AUD-012). Every profile has the optimizer on (AUD-014): unoptimised, `AssetFactory` is right at the 24 576-byte EIP-170 limit, because it embeds the other two contracts. `hardhat.config.ts` reads `TESTNET_RPC_URL` and `PRIVATE_KEY` with `configVariable`, from environment variables or Hardhat's encrypted keystore (`npx hardhat keystore set PRIVATE_KEY`). Nothing loads a `.env` file automatically; [`.env.example`](.env.example) lists the names. Use a testnet burner wallet only.

| [`docs/evidence/`](docs/evidence/) | Evidence runs and per-issue logs |

# AssetToken: Tokenisation Using Blockchain

An academic dApp for NTU SC4053. Authorised issuers tokenise fictional real-world and digital assets as ERC-20 tokens and sell them at a fixed price to whitelisted investors. All ownership records and compliance rules live on Ethereum. The repository is also graded on how the AI-written code was audited, so every change carries an evidence trail (see [Audit trail](#audit-trail)).

**Status (4 November 2026):** contracts, frontend and local tests are complete. Two things remain: a genuine MetaMask browser check ([AUD-002](docs/issues/AUD-002-frontend-dashboards-and-wallet-integration-are-uni.md)) and the public Sepolia deployment ([AUD-003](docs/issues/AUD-003-deployment-and-verification-tooling-are-incomplete.md)).

## What it does

| Contract | Role |
|---|---|
| `AssetFactory` | The platform admin authorises or revokes issuers. An authorised issuer creates an asset, which deploys an `AssetToken` and an `AssetSale` and records them in the registry (`getAsset`, `getAssetCount`). |
| `AssetToken` | A fixed-supply ERC-20 with 0 decimals. Every transfer requires a whitelisted sender and recipient. Revoking an investor keeps their balance but blocks sending, receiving and buying. The issuer can **pause** all token movement and **force-transfer** tokens out of a revoked address, for example to recover a lost key (decision D5). |
| `AssetSale` | Holds sale inventory and sells it at a fixed price, with exact ETH payment. The issuer withdraws proceeds, closes the sale and recovers unsold tokens. ETH forced in from outside can be swept. |

The frontend (React 18, Vite, ethers 6) has a marketplace, an investor portfolio with transfers, issuer and admin dashboards, and on-chain transaction history. The specification is [`docs/spec/spec-v1.md`](docs/spec/spec-v1.md). Where the later phase requirements in [`docs/spec/`](docs/spec/) differ from it, those requirements and their recorded decisions (D1–D10) govern.

## Setup

Validated with Node 22.18.0 (macOS) and Node 24.15.0 with npm 11 (Windows). From the repository root:

```bash
npm ci
npm ci --prefix frontend
npm run compile
```

## Run locally

Use three terminals, all started in the repository root:

```bash
# Terminal 1: leave the local blockchain running
npm run node
```

```bash
# Terminal 2: deploy to that persistent chain and sync ABIs/configuration
npm run deploy:local

# Optional: seed CPT/DLT for exploration, only on an empty local registry
npm run demo:local
```

```bash
# Terminal 3: start the frontend
npm run dev --prefix frontend
```

Open **http://127.0.0.1:5173**. You can browse without a wallet. To sign transactions, connect MetaMask and switch to **Local Ethereum**: chain **31337**, RPC **http://127.0.0.1:8545**, symbol **ETH**. The app offers to add this network when you ask to switch.

Use Hardhat local accounts 0–4 for the admin, the issuer, investor 1, investor 2 and an unapproved investor. Only import these development accounts into a separate development wallet or profile. Hardhat prints their publicly known keys in your terminal; never use them for real funds or commit them. The application never asks for, stores or reads wallet private keys or seed phrases.

Every deployment writes `frontend/src/config/addresses.json` and syncs the three compiled ABIs. After restarting or resetting the chain, deploy again and restart Vite. The app checks the deployment's block hash and runtime bytecode hash, not just its address. `npm run deploy:ephemeral` deploys to a throwaway in-process chain instead.

The UI has no pause or forced-transfer controls (spec-v1 §7 does not require them). The issuer calls them directly on the token contract. Forced transfers do appear in the transaction history.

## Tests

```bash
npm test                              # 132 contract tests
npm test --prefix frontend            # 113 frontend behaviour tests
npm run build --prefix frontend       # TypeScript + production Vite build
npx tsc --noEmit                      # root scripts and contract tests
npm run test:integration              # needs `npm run node` running; deploys its own fixture
bash scripts/evidence.sh <label>      # build, test, gas, coverage (slither if installed) into docs/evidence/runs/
```

The integration suite runs the production frontend services against real local contracts. It signs through an EIP-1193 adapter over Hardhat's unlocked accounts, so it does not test MetaMask. It covers the full lifecycle, including a forced transfer and a pause. The counts above are from 4 November 2026. Contract line coverage is 98.79%.

## Sepolia deployment

```bash
npm run deploy:sepolia
```

This builds with the optimised `production` profile (AUD-012). Every profile has the optimizer on (AUD-014): unoptimised, `AssetFactory` is right at the 24 576-byte EIP-170 limit, because it embeds the other two contracts. `hardhat.config.ts` reads `TESTNET_RPC_URL` and `PRIVATE_KEY` with `configVariable`, from environment variables or Hardhat's encrypted keystore (`npx hardhat keystore set PRIVATE_KEY`). Nothing loads a `.env` file automatically; [`.env.example`](.env.example) lists the names. Use a testnet burner wallet only.

## Audit trail

AI tools (Claude Code, Codex, claude.ai) wrote most of the code. [`CLAUDE.md`](CLAUDE.md) sets the rules every AI session follows, including rules learned from each audit finding.

| Where | What |
|---|---|
| [`docs/issues/INDEX.md`](docs/issues/INDEX.md) | AUD-001 to AUD-014. Each defect has a failing test commit, a fix commit, before/after evidence and an analysis of why the AI made the mistake |
| [`docs/ai-logs/INDEX.md`](docs/ai-logs/INDEX.md) | Every AI session: tool, model, context given and outcome. Transcripts are in `docs/ai-logs/raw/` (emails and Hardhat dev keys redacted, decisions D9 and D10) |
| Tags `spec-v0`, `ai-baseline-phase2`, `-phase3`, `-phase4`, `-d5` | The pre-AI spec, and each first complete AI generation, never edited afterwards |
| [`docs/evidence/`](docs/evidence/) | Evidence runs and per-issue logs |
| [`docs/report/REPORT-MAP.md`](docs/report/REPORT-MAP.md) | Which evidence backs each section of the AI Audit Report |

Commit prefixes show who wrote what: `ai:`, `human:`, `test(AUD-NNN):`, `fix(AUD-NNN):`, `docs:`, `evidence:`, `chore:`. Implementation notes: [Phase 2](docs/phase2-implementation.md), [Phase 3](docs/phase3-implementation.md), [Phase 4](docs/phase4-implementation.md), [D5](docs/d5-implementation.md).

Academic demonstration only. Assets and token prices are simulated. Tokens do not represent legally enforceable ownership or investment claims.

# AssetToken: Tokenisation Using Blockchain

An academic dApp for NTU SC4053. Authorised issuers tokenise fictional real-world and digital assets as ERC-20 tokens and sell them at a fixed price to whitelisted investors. All ownership records and compliance rules live on Ethereum. The repository is also graded on how the AI-written code was audited, so every change carries an evidence trail (see [Audit trail](#audit-trail)).

**Status (4 November 2026):** contracts, frontend and local tests are complete. Two things remain: a genuine MetaMask browser check ([AUD-002](docs/issues/AUD-002-frontend-dashboards-and-wallet-integration-are-uni.md)) and the public Sepolia deployment ([AUD-003](docs/issues/AUD-003-deployment-and-verification-tooling-are-incomplete.md)).

## What it does

| Contract | Role |
|---|---|
| `AssetFactory` | The platform admin authorises or revokes issuers. An authorised issuer creates an asset, which deploys an `AssetToken` and an `AssetSale` and records them in the registry (`getAsset`, `getAssetCount`). |
| `AssetToken` | A fixed-supply ERC-20 with 0 decimals. Every transfer requires a whitelisted sender and recipient. Revoking an investor keeps their balance but blocks sending, receiving and buying. The issuer can **pause** all token movement and **force-transfer** tokens out of a revoked address, for example to recover a lost key (decision D5). |
| `AssetSale` | Holds sale inventory and sells it at a fixed price, with exact ETH payment. The issuer withdraws proceeds, closes the sale and recovers unsold tokens. ETH forced in from outside can be swept. |

The frontend (React 18, Vite, ethers 6) has a marketplace, an investor portfolio with transfers, issuer and admin dashboards, and on-chain transaction history. The specification is [`docs/spec/spec-v1.md`](docs/spec/spec-v1.md). Where the later phase requirements in [`docs/spec/`](docs/spec/) differ from it, those requirements and their recorded decisions (D1–D10) govern.

## Setup

Validated with Node 22.18.0 (Phase 4 session) and Node 24.15.0 with npm 11.12.1 on Windows. From the repository root:

```bash
npm ci
npm ci --prefix frontend
npm run compile
```

## Run locally

Use three terminals, all started in the repository root:

```bash
# Terminal 1: leave the local blockchain running
npm run node
```

```bash
# Terminal 2: deploy to that persistent chain and sync ABIs/configuration
npm run deploy:local

# Optional: seed CPT/DLT for exploration, only on an empty local registry
npm run demo:local
```

```bash
# Terminal 3: start the frontend
npm run dev --prefix frontend
```

Open **http://127.0.0.1:5173**. You can browse without a wallet. To sign transactions, connect MetaMask and switch to **Local Ethereum**: chain **31337**, RPC **http://127.0.0.1:8545**, symbol **ETH**. The app offers to add this network when you ask to switch.

Use Hardhat local accounts 0–4 for the admin, the issuer, investor 1, investor 2 and an unapproved investor. Only import these development accounts into a separate development wallet or profile. Hardhat prints their publicly known keys in your terminal; never use them for real funds or commit them. The application never asks for, stores or reads wallet private keys or seed phrases.

Every deployment writes `frontend/src/config/addresses.json` and syncs the three compiled ABIs. After restarting or resetting the chain, deploy again and restart Vite. The app checks the deployment's block hash and runtime bytecode hash, not just its address. `npm run deploy:ephemeral` deploys to a throwaway in-process chain instead.

The UI has no pause or forced-transfer controls (spec-v1 §7 does not require them). The issuer calls them directly on the token contract. Forced transfers do appear in the transaction history.

## Tests

```bash
npm test                              # 132 contract tests
npm test --prefix frontend            # 113 frontend behaviour tests
npm run build --prefix frontend       # TypeScript + production Vite build
npx tsc --noEmit                      # root scripts and contract tests
npm run test:integration              # needs `npm run node` running; deploys its own fixture
bash scripts/evidence.sh <label>      # build, test, gas, coverage (slither if installed) into docs/evidence/runs/
```

The integration suite runs the production frontend services against real local contracts. It signs through an EIP-1193 adapter over Hardhat's unlocked accounts, so it does not test MetaMask. It covers the full lifecycle, including a forced transfer and a pause. The counts above are from 4 November 2026. Contract line coverage is 98.79%.

## Sepolia deployment

```bash
npm run deploy:sepolia
```

This builds with the optimised `production` profile (AUD-012). Every profile has the optimizer on (AUD-014): unoptimised, `AssetFactory` is right at the 24 576-byte EIP-170 limit, because it embeds the other two contracts. `hardhat.config.ts` reads `TESTNET_RPC_URL` and `PRIVATE_KEY` with `configVariable`, from environment variables or Hardhat's encrypted keystore (`npx hardhat keystore set PRIVATE_KEY`). Nothing loads a `.env` file automatically; [`.env.example`](.env.example) lists the names. Use a testnet burner wallet only.

**What Phase 5 will need** (also listed in AUD-003):
- **A Sepolia RPC endpoint.** A free Alchemy or Infura account gives you one in a few minutes, and keyless public endpoints work too.
- **A funded Sepolia burner wallet** for the platform admin, with ETH from a faucet.
- **Two or more further burner wallets** for the issuer and investors. The demo script `setupDemo.ts` needs three signers, but the Sepolia config has only one, so that config needs extending.
- **You, to run the deploy command.** I don't read `.env`, so the command in the README's "Sepolia deployment" section has to be run outside this session.

The AUD-003 commit is local only, so `main` is 1 commit ahead of GitHub. Before pushing it, I'll re-scan this session's transcript as usual. Want me to push it now?

# Project rules for Claude Code

This repo is graded on two things: the dApp, and how well we audit the code AI tools wrote for it. The process below exists so every claim in our AI Audit Report has evidence behind it. Follow it even when it feels slower.

## Before writing any code

- Read `docs/spec/spec-v1.md` first.
- If it still contains `TODO(decision)` markers, the spec is not frozen. Do not write contract code. Say which decisions are still open and stop.
- Every function you write must trace to a section of the spec. If the spec is silent or ambiguous on something you need, stop and ask. Do not invent requirements.

## Branches and tags

- Never commit to, rebase, or rewrite the `ai-baseline` branch, or move the `spec-v0` or `ai-baseline` tags.
- Never amend published commits or force-push.

## When a bug, vulnerability or spec gap is found

1. Run `scripts/new-issue.sh "<short title>"`. This creates `docs/issues/AUD-NNN-*.md`.
2. Write a regression test that FAILS on the current code. Commit it alone as `test(AUD-NNN): ...`.
3. Run `scripts/evidence.sh AUD-NNN-before`.
4. Fix the code. Commit as `fix(AUD-NNN): ...`.
5. Run `scripts/evidence.sh AUD-NNN-after`.
6. Fill in all four sections of the issue file. Do not set Status to fixed without both evidence runs.

In "Why the AI made the mistake", only state what the transcript or code shows. If you are guessing, start the line with `Hypothesis:`.

## Secrets

- Never read `.env` or print private keys, RPC keys or API keys. AI transcripts in this repo are committed to git.
- Only testnet burner wallets are used in this project.

## Commit message prefixes

| Prefix | Use for |
|---|---|
| `ai:` | Code generated by an AI tool and committed with little or no human change |
| `human:` | Code written or substantially rewritten by a person |
| `test(AUD-NNN):` | Regression test for an issue |
| `fix(AUD-NNN):` | Fix for an issue |
| `docs:` | Spec, report, issue files |
| `evidence:` | Evidence runs, testnet logs |
| `chore:` | Tooling and config |

## Rules learned from audit findings

Append a rule here each time an audit finding shows the AI making a mistake it could repeat. Every rule must cite the issue it came from. This section is part of our specification engineering evidence, so never delete old rules; mark them superseded instead.

- AUD-004: A whitelist mapping alone does not restrict ERC-20 movement. Enforce sender and recipient eligibility in OpenZeppelin's transfer hook and execute a direct-transfer regression; skipped tests are not passing behavioral evidence. Apply the latest explicit requirements when revocation semantics differ from the historical spec.
- AUD-005: Before testing an invariant, check it against every later requirements file. If a later requirement makes it false, restate it in the spec in the same change. Never name a test after an invariant unless the test would fail when that invariant is broken.
- AUD-006: A stored `issuer` or owner field is not proof of authority. Test every role path that touches it (grant, revoke, renounce, hand-over) and any state, such as escrowed tokens, that becomes unrecoverable when the role is gone.
- AUD-007: "No `receive`/`fallback`" does not mean "cannot receive ETH": `selfdestruct` and coinbase rewards force it in. For every contract that holds ETH, test forced ETH, and provide a way to recover any balance above what is owed.
- AUD-008: Implement each function against both the §5 function table and the §3 roles table. A role restriction stated only in §3 is still a revert condition.
- AUD-006, AUD-007: Write a regression's behaviour assertion first and await it (e.g. `await expect(tx).to.revert(ethers)`), then assert the error name. A test that fails only because an error or function is missing from the ABI does not show a behavioural failure, and an un-awaited transaction can leak into the next test.
- AUD-009: Preserve multi-transaction form input across public registry refreshes. Separately invalidate account-dependent data on wallet/chain changes; test approval and deposit as two consecutive user actions.
- AUD-010: A receipt timeout is not a failed transaction. Preserve its hash, keep duplicate submission blocked, and verify an actual receipt before reporting success or a revert.
- AUD-011: An `npm ci` that passes proves the lockfile works only on the machine that wrote it. After any dependency change, keep `test/FrontendLockfile.regression.test.ts` passing (every optional dependency has a lock entry). Do not claim a clean install for other platforms unless one was actually run there.
- AUD-012: A passing test suite does not show that the code has room to grow. Before tagging any change to a contract that `AssetFactory` deploys, record the runtime bytecode size of all three contracts against the EIP-170 limit (24 576 bytes) in the evidence. Deploy to public networks only with the optimised `production` profile.
- AUD-013: Adding an event or a new path that emits an existing event changes what every log consumer shows. When a contract change adds either, find each frontend or script that reads that contract's events, and test that it labels the new operation correctly.
- AUD-014: A fix for one path of a shared risk leaves the risk on every other path. When a fix is scoped to one script, network or profile, list every other path that builds or runs the same code, and test them all, or record each one left open as an issue. Keep the optimizer on in every build profile, because `AssetFactory` embeds two other contracts.

> Phase 4 update (28 October 2026): the current reproducible setup is in [README.md](README.md) and [the Phase 4 workflow](docs/phase4-implementation.md#reproducible-local-workflow). This file retains historical Phase 1 setup notes; use the current instructions for persistent localhost deployment, ABI sync, and frontend tests.

# Setting up the evidence pipeline

Do the steps in order. Step 2 has to happen before any AI tool touches the repo.

## 0. Installs (each teammate, once)

- Git and Python 3.8 or newer
- Foundry: `curl -L https://foundry.paradigm.xyz | bash`, then `foundryup`
- Slither: `python3 -m pip install slither-analyzer`
- Your git name, which is recorded on every evidence run and AI session: `git config --global user.name "Your Name"`

If `python3` is not the command for Python on your machine, change the two `"python3"` entries in `.claude/settings.json`.

## 1. Create the repo

Make it a **private** GitHub repo. AI transcripts are committed, and they can contain anything that was typed into a session. Clone it.

## 2. Commit spec v0 first, on its own

Unzip this kit into the repo root. Fill in "Date written" and "Written by" in `docs/spec/spec-v0.md`. Then:

```bash
git add docs/spec/spec-v0.md
git commit -m "docs: spec v0 (pre-AI proposal)"
git tag spec-v0
git add -A
git commit -m "chore: evidence pipeline"
git push --follow-tags
```

Be honest about what this proves. Git commit dates can be set to anything, so the tag alone is weak evidence. The strong evidence is the date you submitted the BYOP proposal to the coordinator, so put that date in the file.

## 3. Log today's research chat

Copy the claude.ai conversation from 23 Oct 2026 into `docs/ai-logs/exports/2026-10-23-claude-ai-research.md`. Its row in `docs/ai-logs/INDEX.md` is already filled in.

## 4. Start Claude Code and check the hook

From the repo root run `claude -n toolchain-setup`. Accept the trust prompt for the folder if one appears. Run `/hooks`: it should list a `Stop` hook and a `SessionEnd` hook from project settings. After Claude's first reply, `docs/ai-logs/raw/` should contain a `.jsonl` file. If it doesn't, stop and fix that first, because every session before the fix is lost evidence.

## 5. Paste this prompt into Claude Code

```text
Read CLAUDE.md first. Set up the Foundry toolchain for this repo. Do not write any contract code: spec-v1 is not frozen.

1. Check that forge and slither are installed (forge --version, slither --version). If either is missing, stop and tell me. Don't install them yourself.
2. Run `forge init --force` in the repo root. Then run `git status` and make sure it did not change .gitignore, CLAUDE.md, SETUP.md, slither.config.json, or anything under docs/, scripts/ or .claude/. Restore anything it changed.
3. Install OpenZeppelin Contracts pinned to the latest v5.x release tag. Find the tag with `git ls-remote --tags https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts`, then `forge install OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts@<tag>`. Write remappings with `forge remappings > remappings.txt`.
4. Make the scripts executable: chmod +x scripts/*.sh .claude/hooks/archive_transcript.py
5. Run `scripts/evidence.sh pipeline-check` and show me summary.txt. build, test, gas and coverage should exit 0. Slither exits non-zero only if it reports findings.
6. Delete src/Counter.sol, test/Counter.t.sol and script/Counter.s.sol so the AI baseline starts from an empty src/.
7. Commit everything as "chore: foundry toolchain and OpenZeppelin <tag>". Do not push.

Then tell me what you did and anything that did not go as described.
```

## 6. After the session

Run `/export docs/ai-logs/exports/<date>-toolchain-setup.txt` before you quit. Add a row to `docs/ai-logs/INDEX.md`. Commit and push.

## Later: creating the AI baseline

Once `spec-v1.md` has no `TODO(decision)` left, generate the first full version of the contracts on its own branch and freeze it:

```bash
git switch -c ai-baseline
# ...AI generates the code; commit it as-is with an "ai:" prefix...
git tag ai-baseline
git switch main
git merge ai-baseline
```

All review and fixes happen on `main`. `ai-baseline` is never edited again; it is your Report Section 4 and the "before" for every issue.

## Notes

- `forge init` also adds a GitHub Actions workflow in `.github/workflows/`. Keep it. CI runs on GitHub's servers give you timestamped test results that nobody on the team can edit. Its `forge fmt --check` step will fail on unformatted code; run `forge fmt` before pushing.
- Slither does not catch everything. In testing this kit, a function that let anyone whitelist themselves passed Slither with no warning; only a unit test caught it. Tests are the main line of defence and Slither is a supplement.

Use four distinct MetaMask accounts.

| Wallet | Assigned role |
|---|---|
| A | Platform administrator |
| B | Authorised issuer |
| C | Approved investor |

content.text: The code side is ready. What's left are four decisions where the Phase 5 brief conflicts with the current code or is ambiguous. CLAUDE.md says to ask rather than guess:

questions.question: Task 5.2 says the deploy script 'runs the demo setup using testnet wallets', but Task 5.1 is the live MetaMask demo starting from 'A authorises B'. If the script runs the setup on the factory the frontend uses, the live demo has nothing left to do. Which approach?

options.label: Clean + scripted replay (Recommended)
options.description: The deploy script deploys the main factory (Wallet A = admin) and writes the frontend config, leaving the factory empty for the live MetaMask demo. A separate script replays all 12 steps on its own factory with the 4 testnet wallets, giving reproducible tx hashes for the report.

options.label: Pre-run part on main factory
options.description: The script authorises B, creates CPT and funds 5,000 on the main factory. The live MetaMask demo starts at 'B whitelists C'.

options.label: Deploy only
options.description: The script deploys and configures only. All 12 steps are done by hand in MetaMask. Does not meet 'runs the demo setup' literally.

questions.question: How should scripts get the four testnet wallets? Today the Sepolia config has one key (PRIVATE_KEY), and setupDemo.ts needs at least three.

options.label: Four named variables (Recommended)
options.description: SEPOLIA_KEY_A to SEPOLIA_KEY_D, read with configVariable from environment variables or Hardhat's keystore. Wallet A deploys and becomes admin. The same four accounts are imported into MetaMask.

options.label: Admin key only
options.description: Only Wallet A's key is given to scripts. B, C and D exist only in MetaMask, so any scripted replay must stop after deployment.

options.description: The live demo shows the UI's error (screenshot). The scripted replay also sends the transfer directly with a fixed gas limit, so a reverted transaction with RecipientNotWhitelisted is on Etherscan.

options.label: UI block only
options.description: A screenshot of the UI error is the evidence. No on-chain failed transaction.

options.label: Let the UI submit it
options.description: Change the frontend to skip its eligibility preflight for this case so MetaMask submits a transaction that reverts. Changes Phase 4 behaviour and costs gas.

options.label: Fold into Task 5.1

## Decisions made by the user (4 November 2026)

Claude Code raised these conflicts between this request and the current code before any Phase 5 code was written. Claude Code proposed each option, and the user chose the recommended one each time. Numbering continues from D1–D10 in [phase3-requirements.md](phase3-requirements.md).

| # | Question | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| D11 | Task 5.2 says the deploy script "runs the demo setup using testnet wallets", but Task 5.1's live MetaMask demo starts from "Wallet A authorises Wallet B". Running the setup on the factory the frontend uses would leave the live demo nothing to do. | **Clean factory plus scripted replay.** The deployment script deploys the main factory, with Wallet A as platform administrator, saves the factory address, chain ID and ABIs, and configures the frontend. It leaves the factory empty for the live Task 5.1 demo. A separate replay script runs all 12 Task 5.1 steps on its own factory with the four testnet wallets, producing reproducible transaction hashes for the report. |
| D12 | The Sepolia network config has one key (`PRIVATE_KEY`), and `setupDemo.ts` needs at least three signers. Task 5.1 uses four wallets. | **Four named variables:** `SEPOLIA_KEY_A` to `SEPOLIA_KEY_D`, read with `configVariable` from environment variables or Hardhat's keystore, never from a committed file. Wallet A deploys and is the platform administrator. The same four accounts are imported into MetaMask. This replaces `PRIVATE_KEY` for Sepolia, and README and AUD-003 must be updated when it is implemented. |
| D13 | Scenario 7 ("Wallet C tries transferring 20 CPT to Wallet D; transaction fails"): the frontend checks the recipient's eligibility before asking MetaMask to sign (`frontend/src/services/blockchain.ts:310`), so no transaction or hash exists. | **UI block plus on-chain revert.** The live demo records the UI's rejection (screenshot). The replay script also sends the same transfer directly, with a fixed gas limit so that gas estimation does not stop it, so a reverted transaction (`RecipientNotWhitelisted`) is recorded on Sepolia. The frontend's preflight is unchanged. |
| D14 | Phase 4's 13 manual MetaMask and browser scenarios (`docs/phase4-implementation.md`) are all Pending, and the roadmap says not to start a phase before the previous phase's acceptance criteria are met. | **Local rehearsal first.** Before any Sepolia transaction, run Phase 4's manual checklist with MetaMask on the local chain and record the results and screenshots as Phase 4 acceptance (AUD-002). Then run Task 5.1 on Sepolia. |

Still open (not blocking the start of Phase 5):
- "Working deployed application": whether the frontend must be hosted publicly or only run locally against the Sepolia contracts.
- The frontend's read RPC (`VITE_RPC_URL`) is compiled into the browser bundle. It must be a keyless public endpoint, or a key the team accepts as public.

# SC4053 Blockchain Technology — Phase 5: End-to-End Integration and Testnet Deployment

The text below is the user's Phase 5 request, given to Claude Code on 4 November 2026 (session 069871d2). The table and checklist formatting were lost when it was pasted and are restored as Markdown; the wording is unchanged. Decisions raised by Claude Code about conflicts with the current code and earlier specs are in the final section.

---

Deliverable: Working deployed application + reproducible demo

Objective: Ensure the complete application works when all contracts, wallets and interfaces interact.

## Task 5.1 — Run the complete demonstration

Use four distinct MetaMask accounts.

| Wallet | Assigned role |
|---|---|
| A | Platform administrator |
| B | Authorised issuer |
| C | Approved investor |
| D | Initially unapproved investor |

Run these scenarios in order:

Integration test checklist

- [ ] Wallet A authorises Wallet B as an asset issuer
- [ ] Wallet B creates Campus Property Token with 10,000 units
- [ ] Wallet B approves the sale contract and deposits 5,000 units
- [ ] Wallet B whitelists Wallet C
- [ ] Wallet C purchases 100 CPT for 0.1 testnet ETH
- [ ] Portfolio dashboard displays Wallet C's 100 CPT
- [ ] Wallet C tries transferring 20 CPT to Wallet D; transaction fails
- [ ] Wallet B whitelists Wallet D
- [ ] Wallet C transfers 20 CPT to Wallet D successfully
- [ ] Portfolio and event history show 80 CPT for C and 20 CPT for D
- [ ] Wallet B withdraws the ETH proceeds
- [ ] Wallet B creates a second asset and verifies separate balances

This should become your main evaluation demonstration.

## Task 5.2 — Deploy contracts to Sepolia

Create a deployment script that:

- Deploys the factory.
- Assigns the initial platform administrator.
- Saves the factory address, chain ID and contract ABIs.
- Runs the demo setup using testnet wallets.
- Configures the frontend to connect to the deployed addresses.

Keep deployment private keys outside the repository, using environment variables.

## Task 5.3 — Validate security and edge cases

Test unexpected situations, including:

- Wrong network.
- Wallet refuses a transaction.
- Buyer has insufficient ETH.
- Sale inventory is exhausted.
- Purchase amount is zero.
- Recipient is not whitelisted.
- Compliance administrator revokes permission before a transfer.
- An attacker attempts another issuer's administrative functions.
- Issuer withdraws proceeds while no funds remain.
- ETH withdrawal to a contract that rejects payment.

## Phase 5 completion criteria

All core acceptance scenarios succeed on the intended testnet, and the same contract functionality has passing automated tests locally.

Record testnet transaction hashes, test outputs and screenshots. These will become evidence for your final report.

---

## Decisions
